Foreigners can't own land in Thailand. On Koh Samui you can own a condominium unit (within the 49% foreign quota of each building), own a house separately from the land it stands on, or register a lease of land of up to 30 years at the Land Office. Only deal in land with a Chanote (Nor Sor 4 Jor) or a properly surveyed Nor Sor 3 Gor title, and check the island's hillside, height and forest-land rules before you pay anything: authorities raided illegal hillside villas in July 2025 and seized 33 structures on forest land at Overlap Stone 2 in July 2026.

Not legal or financial advice. Last legal review: 2 November 2026. This guide explains the general framework for readers. Thai property law is detailed, enforcement changes, and every plot is different; use an independent licensed Thai lawyer for any purchase or lease, and never rely on the seller's agent or lawyer.

What foreigners can and cannot own

StructureWhat you getMaximum termKey law
Freehold landNot allowed for foreign individuals or foreign-controlled companies (except rare investment approvals)—Land Code
Condominium unitFreehold ownership of the unit and a share of common property, within the 49% foreign quota of the building's total floor areaIndefiniteCondominium Act
Building (house or villa) on leased landOwnership of the structure, registered separately from the landIndefinite for the building; tied to your land rightsCivil and Commercial Code
Registered lease of land or a houseRight to use the property for the lease term30 years per registrationCivil and Commercial Code, section 540
SuperficiesRight to own buildings or plantations on someone else's landUp to 30 years or for lifeCivil and Commercial Code
UsufructRight to use and take the income from a propertyUp to 30 years or for life; ends at deathCivil and Commercial Code
Thai company owning landLegal only if the company is genuinely Thai-controlled and Thai shareholders invest their own money—Foreign Business Act, Land Code

Most foreign buyers on Samui end up with a combination: a registered 30-year land lease, ownership of the villa itself through a building permit in their own name, and sometimes a superficies over the land. A condo is the only true freehold, but Samui has far fewer condo projects than Phuket or Pattaya.

Land titles on Koh Samui

TitleWhat it isSale and lease registrationOur view
Chanote (Nor Sor 4 Jor)Full title deed, surveyed and fixed with numbered boundary markers and GPS-referenced mapsCan be sold, leased and mortgagedThe safest title; insist on it for any significant investment
Nor Sor 3 GorCertificate of use with boundaries surveyed from aerial photographsCan be sold, leased and mortgaged; can be upgraded to a ChanoteAcceptable if surveyed, checked against forest maps and ideally upgraded
Nor Sor 3Certificate of use without an accurate surveySale needs a public notice period at the Land Office before registrationRisky: boundaries and area may be wrong
Sor Kor 1A claim of possession, not a titleCan't normally be sold; generally passes only by inheritanceAvoid
Por Bor Tor 5 / tax receiptsProof that someone paid local tax on the land, not ownershipNo legal transferAvoid
Sor Por Kor 4-01Land-reform land for farmingCan't be sold, except to the state or by inheritance to farming heirsAvoid

Each title type is registered at the Land Office, which can confirm the current owner, encumbrances and any registered leases. [check]

On Samui, the hills and some coastal land were historically state forest or public land. A title, even a Nor Sor 3 Gor, has been revoked in the past where it was found to overlap forest or public land, which is why a lawyer's check against the forest maps matters as much as the title type.

How a 30-year lease works

A lease is the most common way foreigners hold land on Samui. Under section 540 of the Civil and Commercial Code, a lease of immovable property can't exceed 30 years; a longer term is cut back to 30.

  • Registration: leases of more than 3 years must be in writing and registered at the Land Office, with the lease recorded on the back of the title deed. An unregistered long lease is only enforceable for 3 years.
  • Fees: the Land Office charges a registration fee of 1% of the total rent for the whole term, plus 0.1% stamp duty. A 30-year lease at 10,000 THB a month (3.6 million THB in total) costs about 39,600 THB to register. The law splits lease costs equally unless the contract says otherwise.
  • Renewals are not guaranteed: "30+30+30" contracts promise renewals, but in Supreme Court case 4655/2566 the court held renewal provisions void because they would get round the 30-year limit. Treat a renewal option as a personal promise by the current landowner, not as secure rights for 90 years.
  • Death and inheritance: a lease is personal to the tenant by default and ends at death, unless it allows subletting and transfer, in which case a 2016 Supreme Court ruling held that heirs keep it for the rest of the term. Draft the lease with this in mind.
  • Selling: you can only "sell" the remaining term if the lease allows assignment, and the buyer gets only what is left.
  • Prepaid rent: most Samui leases are paid upfront. If the landowner sells or mortgages the land, a registered lease survives; an unregistered one may not.

Is there a 99-year lease in Thailand?

No. The idea of letting foreigners lease land for up to 99 years has been proposed several times since 2024 and debated again in 2025 and 2026, but as of November 2026 no law allowing 99-year leases of private land has been passed. Thailand's Finance Ministry has said that no progress has been made on the concept at policy level and that it would need detailed study, legal amendments and public consultation. Treat any seller who offers a "99-year lease" as a red flag: the maximum registered term remains 30 years.

Condominiums

  • Foreign quota: foreigners together may own no more than 49% of the total floor area of the units in a condominium building. Ask the juristic person (the building's management) for a letter confirming the remaining foreign quota before you pay a deposit.
  • Money from abroad: to buy in a foreign name, the purchase money must be brought into Thailand from abroad in foreign currency and converted to THB by a Thai bank. Ask the bank for the foreign exchange certificate (often called the FET form) for each transfer; the Land Office needs it at registration. [check]
  • Registered condo only: some Samui "condos" are apartment buildings or villa estates not registered under the Condominium Act, so units can't be sold freehold to foreigners. Check the building's condominium registration.
  • Common fees: expect a monthly or annual common-area fee and a sinking fund payment at transfer.
  • Rental use: many condo rules ban daily or weekly rentals; see "Renting your villa out" below.

Thai companies and nominees

For years, some Samui villas were sold through Thai limited companies in which Thai "shareholders" held 51% on paper but put in no money and had no real control. This is a nominee structure, and it is illegal under the Foreign Business Act and the Land Code. The risks:

  • Criminal liability for the foreigner, the nominees and any lawyer who set it up.
  • Orders to dispose of the land, with little say over the price.
  • No protection if the Thai shareholders or directors fall out with you.
  • Closer checks by the Land Office, which asks where Thai shareholders' money came from, and joint enforcement operations on the island.

Joint raids on Samui hillside villas in July 2025 included checks for possible nominee ownership and Foreign Business Act breaches. A properly run Thai company with a genuine business, such as a hotel, is legal; a shell company created only to hold your house is not.

Usufruct, superficies and buying through a Thai spouse

  • Usufruct: the right to live in or rent out a property and keep the income, registered on the title for up to 30 years or for life. It ends at death and can't be inherited. Often used by a foreign partner over land owned by a Thai spouse or partner.
  • Superficies: the right to own buildings on someone else's land, registered for up to 30 years or for life. It can pass to heirs unless the deed says otherwise, and it is often combined with a lease so that the villa itself is clearly yours.
  • Thai spouse: a Thai national married to a foreigner can buy land in their own name. At the Land Office, the foreign spouse usually signs a declaration that the money is the Thai spouse's own property and that the foreigner has no claim to the land. The land belongs to the Thai spouse; in a divorce or death, the foreign spouse has no ownership right to it.

Combinations of lease, superficies and usufruct are common, but each adds cost and complexity. Have a lawyer explain what happens in every scenario: divorce, death of either party, sale of the land and default on a mortgage.

Budget another 1–2% of the price for legal due diligence, translation and contract drafting. Agents' commission (commonly 3–5%) is normally paid by the seller. [check]

Who pays what is a matter of agreement; put it in the sale contract.

Annual Land and Building Tax

Land and Building Tax is assessed every year by the local authority, on Samui the city municipality, on the official appraised value. Bills are normally due in April, and the 2026 deadline was extended to June.

UseRate on appraised value
Main residence: land and house owned by an individual named in the house registrationFirst 50 million THB exempt; then 0.03–0.1%
Main residence: house only (for example a villa on leased land or a condo)First 10 million THB exempt; then 0.02–0.1%
Other residential (second homes, holiday homes)0.02% up to 50 million THB, rising to 0.1% above 100 million THB
Commercial and "other use", including holiday rentals0.3% up to 50 million THB, rising to 0.7% for the highest values
Agricultural land owned by individualsFirst 50 million THB exempt; then 0.01–0.1%
Vacant or unused land0.3–0.7%, plus 0.3% for every 3 years it stays unused, up to 3%

A villa let to holidaymakers is usually assessed as commercial use, which costs far more than residential. Whether a foreign owner of a house or condo qualifies for the main-residence exemption depends on being listed in the house registration; ask the municipality or your lawyer. [check]

Hillside, coastal and forest-land rules on Samui

Samui is an environmental protection area. A Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment notification issued under the Environmental Quality Act, published on 21 May 2025 and in force from 22 May 2025 until 21 May 2030, sets the rules for Samui, Koh Phangan and Koh Tao, alongside the Koh Samui municipal building ordinance.

RuleWhat it means
Elevation 80–140 m above sea levelSingle detached houses only, maximum 6 m high, with at least half of the plot left open
Above 140 mSingle detached houses only, maximum 6 m, with at least 70% of the plot left open
Slopes of 35% or more (below and above 80 m)Single detached house only, 6 m maximum height; footprint capped at 90 m² on plots over 100 square wah (70 m² on smaller plots); limits on cut and fill and regrading
TreesOn steep slopes, trees above a set girth must not be damaged
Small islands (Zone 4)6 m height, buildings at least 10 m back from the shoreline, small floor areas
Hotels and condos near the seaAny hotel or condominium within 50 m of the shoreline needs a full environmental impact assessment, as do those with 80 or more rooms or 4,000 m² or more
Municipal ordinanceA general 12 m building height limit and stricter rules in a 200 m coastal band

Enforcement has been real. On 24 July 2025 a multi-agency team raided eight villas at Khao Laem Yai in Maenam and nearby, citing buildings over the 6 m height limit, deviations from approved plans and construction on 35–50% slopes, and referred the cases to the provincial police. On 22 July 2026 the Royal Forest Department raided Overlap Stone 2 above Maret, found structures on about 4 rai 3 ngan (roughly 7,700 m²) of forest land under the Forest Act 1941, and seized 33 structures; the case went to Bo Phut police.

Before you buy or lease hillside land, have a surveyor confirm the elevation and slope, have your lawyer check the plot against forest and public-land maps, and get written confirmation from the municipality of what can be built. A villa that exceeds the rules can be ordered demolished, whoever built it.

Water, electricity and road access

  • Electricity: supplied by the Provincial Electricity Authority (PEA). A new connection to a remote plot can mean paying for poles and a transformer; ask the PEA office for a quote before you commit.
  • Water: mains water does not reach every part of Samui, and many villas rely on wells, rainwater tanks or delivered water, which can run short in the dry season from February to April. Ask how the property gets water and test the supply. [check]
  • Road access: confirm there is a legal, registered right of way to a public road, not just a track across a neighbour's land. Many hillside roads are steep concrete that is dangerous in the rain and can wash out from October to December.
  • Drainage and landslips: look at the site in the rainy season if you can. Cut slopes without proper retaining walls are a common problem.
  • Internet: fibre reaches most of the main areas; check coverage at the plot.

Does owning property give you a visa?

No. Buying a condo or leasing land on Samui doesn't by itself give you the right to live in Thailand. You still need a visa that fits your situation: a retirement or marriage visa, a Destination Thailand Visa for remote work, or a work visa. The Long-Term Resident (LTR) visa's wealthy global citizen category is the exception that links to investment: it requires at least USD 500,000 invested in Thailand, which can include Thai property, plus at least USD 1 million in assets. Compare the options on our Thailand visa guide and the immigration office guide.

Renting your villa out

  • Short stays need a licence: under the Hotel Act, renting rooms or a house for stays of less than 30 days is treated as a hotel business and needs a hotel licence, unless the property qualifies for the exemption for very small accommodation. Unlicensed short-term letting can be fined and closed. [check]
  • Condos: courts have held that daily and weekly condo rentals breach the Hotel Act, and many buildings ban them in their rules.
  • Taxes: rental income is taxable in Thailand, and a holiday-let villa is usually taxed as commercial use under the Land and Building Tax.
  • TM.30: whoever manages the property must notify immigration within 24 hours of any foreign guest arriving; fines run up to 2,000 THB per late notification.
  • Work permits: running the rental business yourself, including handling guests, is work and may need a work permit; see working on Koh Samui.

Long-term lets of 30 days or more are generally outside the Hotel Act, which is one reason many owners on Samui let by the month or longer.

Buyer's and leaseholder's checklist

  1. Hire your own lawyer, licensed in Thailand and independent of the seller and agent.
  2. Title search at the Land Office: confirm the title type, owner, area, mortgages, existing leases, servitudes and any disputes.
  3. Forest and public-land check: compare the plot with official forest maps and coastal public land.
  4. Survey: have the boundary markers located and the slope and elevation measured.
  5. Zoning and building rules: confirm in writing what can be built, its height and footprint.
  6. Building permit and completion: for an existing villa, check the building permit, the as-built plans and that the house matches them.
  7. Access: a registered right of way to a public road.
  8. Utilities: PEA electricity, water source and capacity, internet.
  9. Company check: if a company is involved, check its shareholders, accounts and whether Thai shareholders invested their own money.
  10. Money trail: bring funds from abroad in foreign currency and keep every bank certificate.
  11. Contracts: lease, superficies, sale agreement and any management agreement in Thai and English, with the Thai version checked by your lawyer.
  12. Exit plan: who can buy it from you later, and what happens on death or divorce.

Never pay a deposit to "hold" a plot before your lawyer has completed the title search, and never sign a Thai-only document you haven't had translated. Spending a few weeks on the island before you buy is the best due diligence of all. Many buyers rent first; see Koh Samui villas for a holiday villa while you look.

Renting long-term instead

For many people, renting is the better choice: no legal risk, no capital tied up, and freedom to move if the area, the road or the neighbours don't suit you. Long-term villa rents start at around 40,000 THB a month, and our partners' long-term villas are monthly rent on request with a minimum of 6 months. See long-term villas and our full long-stay guide for contracts, deposits and bills.
